title: When the Witness Breaks
premise: Yara Joubert, a night-shift dispatcher who has spent years making herself unnoticeable, has privately solved three deaths the police ruled accidental—each time by noticing what the case files missed. When a fourth victim is found wearing clothes stolen from Yara's own closet, it becomes clear someone has been watching her watch everyone else. As Yara races to identify a killer who seems to know her methods, her history, and even her old case notes better than she does, she uncovers that the killer is connected to the very first death she ever solved—a fire ten years ago that Yara survived and misremembered. In the end, Yara realizes the killer is her childhood friend Nadia, presumed dead in that same fire, who has been staging murders to force Yara to finally remember the truth: that Yara escaped the blaze because Nadia held the door for her and was left behind. To stop the final killing, Yara must publicly break her own invisibility, testify to what really happened, and accept that survival came at a price someone else paid.
about_author: August Galloway is the pen name of a former emergency-services dispatcher who spent eleven years listening to a city's worst nights through a headset before turning those voices into fiction. They write mysteries about people the world overlooks, insisting that the quietest witnesses are always the most dangerous.

chapters.title: The Frequency of Small Things
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A night shift at Meridian Taxi Dispatch introduces Yara's gift: hearing patterns in routine calls no one else notices. She quietly maps an 'accidental' overdose against cab routes and knows it wasn't one. The beat is quiet competence masking deep loneliness; Yara narrates the city like a chessboard she watches but never touches.

chapters.title: Three Deaths, Filed Away
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, with flashbacks. We learn of the three deaths Yara solved in secret—the drowned jogger, the garage carbon monoxide case, the fall from the Kessler Building—and the notebooks where she keeps them. Emotional beat: pride tangled with fear of being seen. She almost contacts Detective Okafor, then doesn't.

chapters.title: A Body Wearing My Coat
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Called to dispatch a pickup near the river, Yara arrives to find police swarming a scene: a woman strangled, dressed head-to-toe in clothes stolen from Yara's apartment. Detective Amara Okafor notices Yara's reaction. Beat: terror—the invisible woman has been made visible as evidence.

chapters.title: The Interview Room
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor interrogates Yara, who gives careful half-truths while realizing the killer planted her belongings deliberately. Okafor suspects Yara either staged it or is bait. Beat: two sharp women circling each other, each hiding how much they know.

chapters.title: What the Files Don't Say
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Reviewing the fourth victim's file, Yara spots the killer's signature echoing details only present in HER private notebooks about case two. Someone has read them—or written them. Beat: violation and vertigo; her secret archive has become a weapon pointed at her.

chapters.title: The Man Who Rides Nights
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Working dispatch channels, Yara traces a ghost passenger who books rides near each death site under rotating names. She stakes out a fare and glimpses a figure in the back seat wearing a scarf she recognizes—her mother's. Beat: dread sharpening into pursuit.

chapters.title: Okafor's Doubt
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Under pressure from a captain who wants Yara charged, Okafor secretly reopens the three cold cases using Yara's anonymous tips. She finds Yara's reasoning flawless—and increasingly personal. Beat: reluctant alliance forming; Okafor chooses trust over career.

chapters.title: The Fire, Version One
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, heavy flashback. Ten years ago: the Halberd House boarding-home fire Yara survived at nineteen. Her memory is a blur of smoke and a hand on her shoulder pushing her out. Beat: grief surfacing; the reader learns Yara's invisibility began the night she stopped remembering.

chapters.title: Copy of a Copy
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A fifth murder attempt fails—the intended victim survives because Yara's rerouted cab got there first. At the scene, a note addressed to Yara quotes her own notebook verbatim, including a line she never wrote down anywhere. Beat: the killer isn't reading her files; the killer shares her memories.

chapters.title: Nadia
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Digging into Halberd House records, Yara finds a name erased from every account: Nadia Ferreira, listed as deceased in the fire—but no body was ever recovered. Fragments return: a girl who shared her bunk, her secrets, her escape plan. Beat: hope and horror braided together.

chapters.title: The Archive Beneath
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor discovers someone accessed the department's digitized Halberd House file repeatedly from a library terminal—an account tied to a night-shift taxi employee ID that isn't Yara's. Beat: the net tightens around the wrong suspect; Okafor must warn Yara without tipping the captain.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Yara and Okafor's alternating POV. They stage a fake leak: Yara will 'confess' to the murders at a storage unit holding her notebooks. The trap springs on an empty room—the killer knew, again. Beat: frustration curdling into certainty that the enemy is inside their communication loop.

chapters.title: The Passenger Manifest
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Cross-referencing ten years of dispatch logs, Yara finds the ghost passenger's pattern mirrors routes Nadia planned the summer before the fire—their shared map of the city, drawn in a notebook Yara still owns. Beat: devastating recognition; the killer is navigating their childhood.

chapters.title: Smoke in the Memory
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, immersive flashback chapter. Under a therapist's guidance, Yara reconstructs the fire: she froze; Nadia shoved her through the window and stayed behind to hold the door for others who never came. Yara ran and never looked back. Beat: the full truth of her survival—and her abandonment—lands.

chapters.title: Alive
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV (first time). Nadia, disfigured and living under a borrowed identity, explains her logic: if Yara won't remember, Nadia will make the city remember for her—each murder a recreation of a Halberd House detail. Beat: chilling sympathy; the villain believes she is finishing a rescue.

chapters.title: The Sixth Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara decodes Nadia's pattern: the next murder will recreate the fire itself, in the condemned remains of Halberd House, with a victim inside. She also understands the victim is meant to be her. Beat: cold clarity replacing fear; Yara stops running.

chapters.title: Confession, Broadcast
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Knowing Nadia listens to dispatch frequencies, Yara breaks her decade of silence and reads a public confession over the radio: admitting she lived because Nadia didn't, naming her, asking her to come home. Beat: the invisible woman makes herself the loudest voice in the city.

chapters.title: Halberd House Burns Again
chapters.summary: Alternating Yara/Nadia POV. Yara walks into the trap anyway; Nadia locks them both inside the building with accelerant and a timer. Through smoke, they speak face to face for the first time in ten years. Beat: climax begins—two survivors, one debt, flames rising.

chapters.title: The Door
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara refuses to escape alone this time, physically holding the exit open and forcing Nadia to choose. Nadia, broken by being remembered rather than punished, falters. Okafor's units arrive. Beat: the theme made flesh—survival means carrying others out, not leaving them.

chapters.title: Arrest in Daylight
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Nadia surrenders; Okafor takes her statement, which corroborates everything and damns her too. The captain wants Yara charged for obstruction; Okafor argues her testimony solved four murders. Beat: justice arriving imperfectly, with real costs on both sides.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Months later: testimony given, notebooks surrendered, Yara visiting Nadia in custody and beginning the slow work of shared mourning. She keeps dispatching nights but no longer hides. Beat: bittersweet resolution; identity rebuilt not as invisibility but as chosen visibility.

chapters.title: The Last Fare
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, coda. On the anniversary of the fire, Yara takes one final dispatch call from a scared young woman in a burning building and talks her out calmly, then drives her home herself. Beat: closure—the witness who broke is now the voice that holds the door open for strangers.
